the haemodynamic response measured in sensory cortex of alert behaving animals is comprised of at least two distinct components, and that one of these components, a hitherto undescribed signal, is not predictable by standard neural predictors of the haemodynamic signals.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the brain's haemodynamic response and its underlying neural activity.
the relationship between brain activity and brain blood flow, and how this relationship may be altered in disease.
the mechanisms underlying functional brain imaging, in particular functional magnetic resonance imaging, and how these mechanisms are altered in neurological and psychiatric disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between the neuronal activity in the visual cortex and the hemodynamic response in the visual cortex is not as simple as we have been taught to think.
the current understanding of haemodynamics and neuronal activity in V1 is not correct and that a new mechanism is present that is entrained to expected events.
the relationship between haemodynamics and neuronal activity has been shown to be much more complex than previously thought, and this is a significant finding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the haemodynamic response in sensory cortex is more complex and dynamic than previously thought, with the possibility of a preparatory component.
the brain is more than the sum of its parts.

the haemodynamic signals are more complex than what is currently assumed and that there are two independent components: one that can be explained by the metabolic demand of the neuronal activity and one that is driven by the task structure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the haemodynamic response is not a reliable proxy for the underlying neuronal response in V1.
the haemodynamic signals underlying fMRI do not necessarily reflect local neuronal activity.
the haemodynamic response to visual stimulation in the primary visual cortex (the most commonly studied brain region in fMRI studies) is not a simple reflection of local neuronal activity.
